pages.title: Projected, not certified: the House turns, and twelve Senate seats keep counting
Projected, not certified: the House turns, and twelve Senate seats keep counting, continued

projected-not-certified-the-house-turns-.title: Projected, not certified: the House turns, and twelve Senate seats keep counting
projected-not-certified-the-house-turns-.dek: By breakfast in Berlin the networks had called the House for the Democrats. The Senate, a Westchester warehouse and the people who count ballots are still at work, which is how it should be.
projected-not-certified-the-house-turns-.text: At 04:08 Berlin time NBC News projected that the Democrats will win the House of Representatives, on an estimate of about 248 seats, “well beyond the 218 needed” [1]. CBS and ABC made the same call [2][6]. That is a projection, a statistical judgement made in a television studio. The other kind of call goes race by race. By 04:42 CET the Associated Press tally, as relayed by the Azerbaijani agency APA, stood at 111 House seats for the Democrats and 64 for the Republicans [5]. That tally is slower, and it is the one that grows into a certificate. What changed hands is already concrete. In Pennsylvania three Republican incumbents lost: Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th District, Rob Bresnahan in the 8th and Scott Perry in the 10th [1][2]. Elaine Luria won back Virginia’s 2nd, Manny Rutinel took Colorado’s 8th, and Jamie Ager won North Carolina’s 11th, a seat Trump carried by more than 9 points two years ago [1]. Rebecca Bennett ousted Tom Kean Jr. in New Jersey’s 7th [2]. The mid-decade redistricting fight did not decide everything in advance. Democrats held Texas’s redrawn 34th District, two redrawn Florida seats and Alabama’s 2nd [2]. The House the Democrats are winning takes office on 3 January [1]. The Senate is closer. The Republicans went into Tuesday with a 53–47 majority [4]. By 05:14 CET, NBC’s Decision Desk, working from AP data, had the Democrats at 49 seats and the Republicans at 39, with 12 races not yet projected [3]. The four Democratic gains are North Carolina (Roy Cooper), South Carolina (Annie Andrews), Texas (James Talarico) and Ohio (Sherrod Brown, 48.6% to 46.5%) [3][4]. Democrats also held Georgia and New Hampshire [4]. On NBC’s count the Democrats need two more seats for a majority, and a 50–50 tie would be broken by the vice president [3]. The counting is not finished, and the numbers are not settled. In Maine, Susan Collins had 50.3% to Troy Jackson’s 49.6%, with 39% of the vote in. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed had 51.0% to Mike Rogers’s 47.2%, with 31.7% in. Kansas was rated lean Democratic, and Alaska had reported nothing yet [3]. These are partial counts, and this desk does not turn them into results. The most useful words of the night came from the people who lost. “The voters have spoken,” wrote John Cornyn, who lost his primary to Ken Paxton, as he congratulated Talarico and offered help with his transition [4]. Thom Tillis said he looked forward to “working with him during the transition” after Cooper won his seat [4]. In New Hampshire, John Sununu said simply that “it is not our night” [4]. The president wrote that Republicans would have won “IN A LANDSLIDE” had he been on the ballot [6]. Results are rarely changed by speeches. Transitions run on the dull work that comes after them. Then there is the machinery, which is where trust is earned. In Westchester County, New York, which makes up part of the competitive 17th District, scanners rejected ballots all day. The cause was a software update for one municipal contest, made after the machines had been tested; machines elsewhere still ran the old programming [7]. Voters put their ballots into sealed bags. A judge allowed officials to move them to a secure warehouse under police escort, to be scanned under the eyes of party representatives, and the count is expected to take until at least Wednesday [7]. The Republican incumbent, Mike Lawler, put it plainly: “There’s no shenanigans going on here” [7]. In Leavenworth County, Kansas, a clerical error delivered about 100 ballots instead of 1,000 and one polling place stopped voting for about 90 minutes. Three precincts in Chester County, Pennsylvania, opened late and were allowed to stay open 30 minutes longer [8]. The fixes were small, written down and public. That is the system working. On turnout, nobody has a final figure yet, and you should be wary of anyone who claims one. Before Tuesday, more than 57 million Americans had voted early, a midterm record according to University of Florida Election Lab figures. Its director, Michael McDonald, cautioned that an early-vote record is not the same as a turnout record [9]. The rest is paperwork. States canvass, check and certify over the coming weeks, and only then is anything final. A night like this ends with a projection. The work of a democracy ends with a signature.

sixty-days-89-already-on-ordinary-tariff.title: Sixty days, 89% already on ordinary tariffs, and a help desk in Pretoria
sixty-days-89-already-on-ordinary-tariff.dek: Washington has given notice that South Africa and Rwanda will leave its African trade preference scheme. The useful response came from the trade ministry, and it reads like an invoice checklist.
sixty-days-89-already-on-ordinary-tariff.text: On Monday, 2 November, President Trump notified Congress and the governments of South Africa and Rwanda that he intends to remove both countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) as of 1 January 2027 [1]. AGOA is the US preference scheme that gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries generally duty-free access for qualifying goods [2]. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the annual review had found “concerning and pervasive practices”. For South Africa, the administration listed barriers to US trade and investment, corruption and “threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests” [1]. The reply that matters most for businesses came a day later, and it was not a speech. South Africa’s Department of Trade, Industry and Competition published an FAQ for exporters [2]. Its first point is a number. Already 89% of South African exports to the US enter under ordinary WTO most-favoured-nation tariffs, not under AGOA [2]. Its second is a correction to the rumours: exports are not prohibited, and goods keep entering the US as long as they meet the usual customs and safety rules [2]. The notice period also works in both directions. In the ministry’s reading, the government has 60 days to address the issues Washington raised. If it does, South Africa stays in AGOA. If not, it leaves on 1 January [2]. Desk arithmetic: 60 days from 2 November ends on 1 January. Then comes the checklist. Confirm the HS code of each product. Check whether it qualifies for AGOA at all. Look up the MFN rate in the US tariff book. Review contracts and Incoterms. Talk to US buyers, because in the US the importer pays the duty [2]. The ministry lists automotive parts, citrus, wine, macadamia nuts, clothing, chemicals and pharmaceuticals among the sectors that may be exposed, and it adds that “the actual impact will differ significantly” from product to product [2]. It also tells exporters not to leave the US market [2]. If your company buys from South Africa, the useful work this week is ordinary. Find the tariff line, the Incoterm and the clause that says who pays if the duty changes on New Year’s Day.

360-billion-short-and-a-package-due-by-m.title: €360 billion short, and a package due by mid-December
360-billion-short-and-a-package-due-by-m.dek: Brussels is preparing to rework parts of the single market's rulebook to help firms buy from someone other than China.
360-billion-short-and-a-package-due-by-m.text: The European Commission is preparing targeted changes to the rules of its €18 trillion internal market, meant to help EU firms diversify their sourcing away from countries including China, according to people familiar with the work quoted in Bloomberg reporting summarised by Briefs [1]. A Commission spokesperson declined to comment [1]. What is reportedly on the list is the unglamorous kind of thing that changes trade. It includes motor-vehicle type-approval rules, the foreign-subsidies framework, forced-labour provisions and the trade secrets directive [1]. The changes are to be bundled into a package due by mid-December. Its centrepiece is a “diversification instrument” that would map where the EU depends heavily on outside suppliers of goods and services and set out ways to reduce that exposure [1]. A second tool would let Brussels restrict market access for selected goods and services faster, and across a wider scope, than current instruments allow. A solidarity mechanism would set out options if a third country targets one or more member states [1]. The backdrop is a number. The EU’s goods deficit with China was about €360 billion last year, and Eurostat data put it at roughly €361 billion [1]. Separate safeguards for chemicals, furniture and machinery, which could take the form of quotas or tariffs, could come as early as the first quarter of 2027 [1]. Officials are said to be using as a reference a recent arrangement capping Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 a year [1]. None of this is law yet. Trade chief Maroš Šefčovič plans to take stock of talks with Beijing early next year [1]. For a purchasing manager, the useful document is not the headline. It is the dependency map, once it is published.

oil-revenue-down-23-financing-costs-up-3.title: Oil revenue down 23%, financing costs up 38%: Riyadh's quarter
oil-revenue-down-23-financing-costs-up-3.dek: Saudi Arabia's budget report is a ledger of what lower oil income does to a petrostate.
oil-revenue-down-23-financing-costs-up-3.text: Saudi Arabia ran a deficit of SR84.3 billion ($22.38 billion) in the third quarter, according to the Finance Ministry’s quarterly report [1]. Revenue was SR259.1 billion and spending SR343.4 billion [1]. Oil revenue fell 23% from a year earlier to SR116.5 billion, while non-oil revenue rose 20% to SR142.6 billion [1]. Over the first nine months, financing expenses climbed 38% to SR54.8 billion and subsidies 49% to SR41.7 billion [1]. The ministry now estimates a full-year deficit of SR165.4 billion, and in September it projected SR191 billion, or 3.6% of GDP, for 2027 [1]. Desk arithmetic: in the third quarter non-oil income exceeded oil income by SR26.1 billion. That is diversification, and it shows in the ledger, not the speeches.

podium-vs-print-expanding-profitability-.title: Podium vs Print: "expanding profitability" and 55%
podium-vs-print-expanding-profitability-.dek: AMD's chief executive promised growth and fatter profits for years to come. Her own outlook table, printed the same evening, puts next quarter's gross margin a point lower.
podium-vs-print-expanding-profitability-.text: The podium. AMD’s third quarter was the biggest in its history: revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% on a year earlier, above the top of its own guidance [1]. Lisa Su, its chair and chief executive, said the data centre business had nearly doubled and that growth should “accelerate further” in the fourth quarter. Then came the sentence for the long run: AMD is “confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years” [1]. The print. The same release carries an outlook table. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected at about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which would be 66% growth on a year earlier [1]. Non-GAAP gross margin is expected at about 55% [1]. In the third quarter it was 56% [1]. CNBC notes that the 55% sits slightly below the 55.3% analysts had pencilled in, according to StreetAccount [2]. Desk arithmetic: the revenue range runs from about $16.5 billion to $17.5 billion; a one-point lower margin on $17 billion is roughly $170 million of gross profit that the higher revenue has to cover. The gap. It is a small gap, and both statements can be true. Su spoke of “the coming years”; the table speaks of one quarter. Margins can dip while a new product ramps and rise again later. On the call she said AMD had secured “the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components” for much higher growth next year [2], and securing scarce parts is rarely cheap. The release does not say why the margin is guided lower, so neither should we. What the market did. The shares rose about 8% after hours [2]: investors paid for the $17 billion and forgave the point. By early Wednesday in Berlin, though, the election count had taken over, and Nasdaq-100 futures were down about 2% [3]. A record quarter does not insulate a share from the night’s news. For you, the habit is the same as ever: read the outlook table before the quote, and the quote before the price. Nothing here is investment advice.

up-1-5-at-the-open-down-1-5-by-mid-morni.title: Up 1.5% at the open, down 1.5% by mid-morning: Seoul reads the count
up-1-5-at-the-open-down-1-5-by-mid-morni.dek: South Korea's chip shares opened on Wall Street's rally and then traded the American election instead.
up-1-5-at-the-open-down-1-5-by-mid-morni.text: Wednesday began well in Seoul. The Kospi rose 1.48% in early trade [1], helped by Tuesday’s New York session, where the Philadelphia semiconductor index rose 2.64% and AMD 3.65% [2]. Briefly it traded above 5,800 [2]. Then the American count arrived. By about 10:45 local time (02:45 CET) the Kospi was down 1.5% at 5,564.34, after a range of 5,546.89 to 5,828.13 [2]. Foreign investors sold a net 695 billion won of shares; retail investors and institutions bought [2]. SK hynix fell 3.65% and Samsung Electronics 1.82% [2]. Aju Press linked the turn to early results suggesting Democrats could take both chambers of Congress, and to the worry that this might mean tighter oversight of AI data centre building [2]. Tokyo, back from Tuesday’s holiday, opened lower and kept going: the Nikkei 225 was down 3% at 61,183.06 in the same report, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped only 0.3% and Shanghai 0.2% [2]. The won strengthened 0.6% to 1,338.30 per dollar [2]. Desk arithmetic: from the session high of 5,828.13 to 5,564.34 is a fall of about 4.5% inside two hours. Nothing in Korea’s factories changed in those two hours. What changed was a guess about Washington’s next two years, made before the count was finished. For you, that is a reason to read morning moves as opinion, and closing prices as slightly firmer opinion. Nothing here is investment advice.

revenue-up-32-shares-down-8-7-shopify-mi.title: Revenue up 32%, shares down 8.7%: Shopify missed by a rounding error
revenue-up-32-shares-down-8-7-shopify-mi.dek: A one-quarter gap between growth and expectation, measured in the smallest unit Wall Street uses.
revenue-up-32-shares-down-8-7-shopify-mi.text: Shopify’s third-quarter revenue rose 32% to $3.74 billion [2], and its adjusted earnings of 49 cents a share beat estimates of 46 cents [1]. The shares still fell 8.74% on Tuesday [1]. Revenue was just below the $3.75 billion analysts expected; merchandise volume of $119.15 billion missed $120.03 billion; subscription gross profit came in near $20 million short [1]. The company’s president, Harley Finkelstein, called it the 13th straight quarter of volume growth above 20% and said Shopify would “ignore the noise day to day” [1]. Desk arithmetic: on the rounded figures, the revenue miss was about $10 million, roughly 0.3% of the quarter. A business can grow by a third and still disappoint a price that assumed a little more. Nothing here is investment advice.

a-public-health-doctor-in-columbus-and-1.title: A public-health doctor in Columbus, and 15 governors to 10
a-public-health-doctor-in-columbus-and-1.dek: Congress gets the headlines. The statehouses, which run the elections, the Medicaid rolls and the roads, were on the ballot too.
a-public-health-doctor-in-columbus-and-1.text: Thirty-six states elected governors on Tuesday [2]. By 04:42 CET, the Associated Press count, as relayed by the agency APA, gave the Democrats 15 governorships and the Republicans 10, with the rest still to be called [2]. The most telling result came from Ohio. Amy Acton, a Democrat and the former director of the Ohio Department of Health, is projected by ABC News to beat Republican Vivek Ramaswamy [1]. Ohio has chosen a public-health administrator to run the state. California went to Democrat Xavier Becerra, ABC projects [1]. In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff used his own victory speech to congratulate Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democrat who won the governor’s race [3]. Why should you care, sitting in Europe? Because American governors do much of the work that Washington talks about. They run Medicaid enrolment, unemployment offices, the state National Guard when it is not federalised and, not least, the administration of elections. When a county scanner rejects ballots, state and county officials are the ones who sort it out. In many states, the governor also signs or vetoes the congressional map. That matters in a decade when maps have been redrawn mid-cycle. Change in Washington comes through votes in Congress. Change in a state comes through budgets, appointments and an agency head who answers the phone. Neither makes as much noise as the night itself.

mail-down-13-in-person-up-46-how-america.title: Mail down 13%, in person up 46%: how Americans voted early
mail-down-13-in-person-up-46-how-america.dek: The record early vote was not a postal one.
mail-down-13-in-person-up-46-how-america.text: More than 57 million Americans voted before Tuesday, a midterm record on University of Florida Election Lab figures [1]. How they voted changed more than how many did. Across the 27 states and Washington, D.C., that reported both methods in each of the last two midterms, mail voting fell 13% while early in-person voting rose 46% [1]. Texas logged 7.7 million early ballots, 97% of them cast in person [1]. In North Carolina, about 94,000 mail ballots came back, 40% fewer than in 2022. One analyst pointed to a new rule requiring voters to seal an inner envelope, on pain of spoiling the ballot [1]. The lesson is a modest one. Small rules about envelopes shape how a country votes.

the-annex-5-501-people-one-sentence-abou.title: The Annex: 5,501 people, one sentence about violence, and why powerlessness matters more than distrust
the-annex-5-501-people-one-sentence-abou.dek: A four-country survey finds that feeling shut out goes with endorsing political violence, and that feeling powerless makes the link stronger while distrust of institutions makes it weaker.
the-annex-5-501-people-one-sentence-abou.text: The document. “From Grievance to Endorsement: Political Alienation as a Conditional Catalyst, Not a Cause, of Support for Political Violence”, by Tahir Abbas of Aston University, published in Psychology of Violence [1]. It draws on an EU-funded online survey run between 2021 and 2023 with 5,501 adults: 2,535 in the United Kingdom, 1,963 in the Netherlands, 635 in Denmark and 368 in Norway [1]. On the morning after a long night of American counting, it is a useful thing to read slowly. The line. Participants were asked whether they agreed that “Sometimes people need to use violence to achieve their goals.” About 8.5% strongly agreed [1]. The study split people into two broad groups found in every country. The 59% who reported relatively little exclusion and alienation strongly endorsed violence at a rate of 0.5%. Among the other 41%, about 20% did, and roughly four in five did not [1]. Desk arithmetic: 59% × 0.5% plus 41% × 20% comes to about 8.5% of the whole sample, which matches the headline figure. The lines around it. Feeling that your group is excluded, humiliated or treated unfairly went with more endorsement in all four countries [1]. Political alienation on its own did not, once exclusion was taken into account. It changed the strength of the link instead, in two opposite directions. Among people who felt powerless, with lines like “people like me have no power” or “I have no future”, exclusion and endorsement were much more closely tied. Among people who distrusted institutions, the tie was weaker, though still there [1]. Abbas calls alienation “a conditional catalyst, not a cause or a brake” [1]. The caveats. The design cannot show cause and effect. Endorsement was measured with a single statement about attitudes, not behaviour, and most people who hold such views never act on them [1]. All answers were self-reported, the pattern was clearest in the Netherlands, and the results may not travel beyond established democracies [1]. The constructive reading. Distrust, it seems, tends to lead people to walk away rather than lash out. Powerlessness is the more dangerous feeling, and the author suggests that work on people’s sense that they can change outcomes may do more than campaigns for trust alone [1]. He also warns that security measures which make whole communities feel stigmatised could deepen the exclusion at the root [1]. A ballot that gets counted, slowly and in public, is one of the oldest answers to powerlessness we have.

a-calm-room-and-a-playlist-or-an-mri-sca.title: A calm room and a playlist, or an MRI scanner: where psilocybin was taken seemed to matter
a-calm-room-and-a-playlist-or-an-mri-sca.dek: A small Copenhagen study found no overall rise in a marker of brain synapses after one dose, but a difference between settings that its authors call preliminary.
a-calm-room-and-a-playlist-or-an-mri-sca.text: Researchers at Copenhagen University Hospital gave 15 healthy adults a single strong dose of psilocybin and used PET scans to measure SV2A, a protein that serves as an indirect marker of synapses, before the dose and a week after [1]. The study, in Translational Psychiatry , found no statistically significant overall rise. Average changes were around 2% to 3%, and the trial stopped early after an interim analysis showed it was unlikely to reach its target [1]. The more interesting part is exploratory. The first five participants took the drug lying in an MRI scanner; the other ten took it in a dedicated room with a curated playlist, with two facilitators present in both settings [1]. The room group reported more intense mystical-type experiences and more positive lasting effects at three months, with no difference in negative effects [1]. Their SV2A rose by about 5% to 6% in the frontal cortex and hippocampus, while the scanner group showed no increase; the gap between groups was significant only in the frontal cortex [1]. The authors themselves call the setting differences “preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive” [1]. There was no placebo, the groups were not randomised, the scanner group had five people, and some authors have ties to companies developing psychedelic drugs [1]. Still, the old clinical intuition gets a small data point: the room is part of the treatment.

babies-hardly-blink-by-six-some-children.title: Babies hardly blink; by six some children blink 20 times a minute
babies-hardly-blink-by-six-some-children.dek: In 113 Japanese preschoolers, those who blinked more did a little better at switching rules. The researchers say not to use it on your own child.
babies-hardly-blink-by-six-some-children.text: Newborns often blink fewer than five times a minute; adults average around 20 [1]. Researchers from Tsukuba and Kyoto filmed 113 children aged three to six while they played a card-sorting game that switches between colour and shape rules [1]. Children who blinked more sorted more accurately when the rule changed, and the link held after allowing for age, at a modest partial correlation of 0.22 [1]. Blink rate also tracked activity in the upper-right prefrontal cortex, measured with a light-based headband [1]. The study, in Communications Psychology , measured each child once, so it cannot show cause [1]. The authors are blunt: there is no evidence that blinking more helps, and the measure “should not be used to evaluate or diagnose individual children” [1]. A cheap window into development, then, and not a test.

wind-nearly-doubled-on-tuesday-and-the-g.title: Wind nearly doubled on Tuesday, and the gas plants burned 2% less
wind-nearly-doubled-on-tuesday-and-the-g.dek: SMARD's first full-day figures show 368.8 gigawatt hours from the turbines against 196.6 on Monday. The fossil fleet barely noticed, and neither did the price.
wind-nearly-doubled-on-tuesday-and-the-g.text: Yesterday the wind did what Monday’s forecasters promised. German onshore turbines generated 279.3 gigawatt hours across the whole of Tuesday 3 November and offshore wind 89.5, SMARD’s provisional figures show [1]. Desk arithmetic: that is 368.8 gigawatt hours, against 196.6 on Monday (73.7 onshore, 122.9 offshore), an increase of about 88% [1]. Onshore alone produced almost four times Monday’s output [1]. The fossil fleet hardly moved. Natural gas plants produced 310.0 gigawatt hours on Tuesday against 316.3 on Monday, a fall of about 2% [1]. Lignite gave up a little more, 260.5 against 276.1, about 6% [1]. Hard coal went the other way, from 102.3 to 107.7 [1]. Desk arithmetic: the three together fell from 694.7 to 678.2 gigawatt hours, by 16.5, while wind rose by 172.2 [1]. So where did the wind go? Not into a quieter country: total grid load was 1,421.4 gigawatt hours on Tuesday, barely below Monday’s 1,436.7 [1]. SMARD’s residual load, the demand left over after wind and solar, fell from 1,159.8 to 978.3 gigawatt hours [1]. The generation series do not show where the rest of the difference was settled; the cross-border account is a separate ledger, and this desk has not yet checked it. What the figures do show is that one windy weekday does not switch off the plants that were already booked, warmed up and selling into the evening peak. The price said the same thing, a day in advance. Tuesday’s day-ahead average was €252.85 per megawatt hour and Wednesday’s is €248.99, the first delivery day below €250 since 28 October [1]. Desk arithmetic: the windiest day since 27 October was priced only €6.46 below Monday’s €259.31 [1]. The auction had already read the forecast. It priced the wind as a help, not a rescue. None of this argues against turbines. It argues for patience with the figures: the first full-day generation numbers are provisional, they move, and a single day tells you about a single day [1]. Nothing here is investment advice.

brent-at-103-34-near-a-four-week-low-and.title: Brent at $103.34, near a four-week low, and a crude draw nobody expected
brent-at-103-34-near-a-four-week-low-and.dek: Oil slipped in Asian trade while America counted votes. Industry data showed U.S. crude stocks falling by 5.27 million barrels when analysts expected a rise.
brent-at-103-34-near-a-four-week-low-and.text: Oil spent the American election night drifting rather than jumping. Brent futures fell 26 cents, or 0.25%, to $103.34 a barrel by 02:57 CET, and U.S. WTI crude fell 53 cents to $95.56, Reuters reported via CNBC [1]. In Tuesday’s session Brent had already eased more than 1% to its lowest level in nearly four weeks, as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran [1]. The talks are the price. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal, while a U.S. official described “defensive” strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island that another official said did not signal a return to major combat [1]. Qatar has stepped up mediation [1]. Each sentence moves the barrel a little; none of them settles it. The inventories are the invoice. The American Petroleum Institute’s figures, cited by market sources, showed U.S. crude stocks falling by 5.27 million barrels in the week to 30 October [1]. Eight analysts polled by Reuters had expected a rise of about 880,000 barrels [1]. Gasoline stocks rose by 1.43 million barrels and distillates, which include diesel and heating oil, fell by 1.19 million [1]. “Diesel inventories remain tight,” Haitong Futures wrote [1]. That last line is the one that reaches you at the pump and the heating-oil tank. The official U.S. Energy Information Administration figures are due at 16:30 CET today and can confirm or overturn the industry count [1]. Nothing here is investment advice.

voerde-weisweiler-werne-where-rwe-s-back.title: Voerde, Weisweiler, Werne: where RWE's backup megawatts will stand
voerde-weisweiler-werne-where-rwe-s-back.dek: RWE won about 2,100 'reduced megawatts' in Tuesday's auction. The rules count only 85% of a gas plant, so the turbines will be bigger than the headline.
voerde-weisweiler-werne-where-rwe-s-back.text: The first backup-plant auction now has addresses. RWE says it won contracts for three hydrogen-capable gas plants in North Rhine-Westphalia: about 730 megawatts in Voerde, 700 in Weisweiler and 700 in Werne [1]. Those are “reduced megawatts”: under the law, only 85% of a gas plant’s installed capacity counts in the auction [1]. Desk arithmetic: about 2,130 counted megawatts implies roughly 2,500 installed. RWE says it wants to start building the first plant “in a few weeks” and plans to invest about €9 billion by 2031 in flexible generation, batteries and hydrogen production [1]. It runs about 4,200 megawatts of gas plants in Germany today [1]. A press release is a promise; the building site will be the receipt.

4-95-at-tuesday-s-close-about-4-90-by-be.title: 4.95% at Tuesday's close, about 4.90% by Berlin's breakfast
4-95-at-tuesday-s-close-about-4-90-by-be.dek: The bond market did what it usually does on a surprising night: it bought Treasuries, sold the dollar, and left the arguing to the strategists.
4-95-at-tuesday-s-close-about-4-90-by-be.text: On Tuesday, election day, the US Treasury’s official closing yields were 4.61% for the two-year note and 4.95% for the ten-year [1]. That was a touch higher than Monday’s 4.59% and 4.91%, and well below where October began, at 4.78% and 5.24% [1]. The chart shows the month: a slow drift, one sharp drop on 22 October, and a quiet Tuesday. Then the count started. As CNBC’s election desk projected a Democratic House, with the Senate still undecided, investors sold stock futures and bought bonds. By about 04:20 CET the ten-year yield had fallen nearly 5 basis points to 4.902% and the two-year 6 basis points to 4.55%, CNBC reported [2]. Yields fall when prices rise. Those are overnight quotes, not closes, which is why the chart stops at Tuesday. The dollar went the other way. The euro firmed 0.5% to $1.1249, the yen 0.7% to 157.63 per dollar, and the dollar index fell 0.3% to 101.4, Reuters reported [3]. Against the Swiss franc the dollar lost 0.9% [3]. Carol Kong of Commonwealth Bank of Australia said a Democratic sweep “would limit government spending over Trump’s term” [3]. Others were less sure the election was the point at all. “I don’t think the big risk to markets is from the blue wave; it’s investors overreacting to a blue wave,” said Michael Arone of State Street [4]. Tai Hui of J.P. Morgan Asset Management asked how much of the move was politics and how much the AI story of recent weeks, and leaned to the latter [4]. Desk arithmetic: the gap between the ten-year and two-year closed Tuesday at 0.34 percentage points, against 0.46 on 1 October [1]. Overnight, on CNBC’s quotes, it was about 0.35 [2]. In plain terms, the night moved the level of borrowing costs, not their shape. For you, holding euros, a dollar that is 0.5% cheaper makes American goods and holidays slightly cheaper, and dollar savings slightly smaller in euros. Neither is a reason to act before a close. Nothing here is investment advice.

4-to-6-on-15-november-beijing-leans-on-i.title: 4% to 6% on 15 November: Beijing leans on its own currency
4-to-6-on-15-november-beijing-leans-on-i.dek: China's central bank is making banks hold more foreign currency, to slow a yuan that has been rising too fast for its liking.
4-to-6-on-15-november-beijing-leans-on-i.text: Most central banks spend their effort stopping a currency from falling. The People’s Bank of China is trying to stop one rising too fast. On Tuesday it said financial institutions must hold 6% of their foreign-currency deposits as reserves from 15 November, up from 4%, to strengthen “the management of foreign exchange liquidity” [1]. Reuters calculates that this takes about $24 billion out of the system [1]. The reason is in the ledger of trade. The yuan has gained more than 5% against the dollar this year, Reuters reports, to its strongest since 2022, carried by robust exports, big trade surpluses and companies converting their dollar earnings [1]. The onshore yuan had risen for 13 days in a row, the longest run since 1996, before the announcement ended it, according to Bloomberg as cited by CNBC TV18 [2]. On the day it weakened as much as 0.37%, to 6.6728 per dollar [1]; by early Wednesday the offshore rate was 6.6782 [3]. Not everyone expects the step to bite. ANZ’s Zhaopeng Xing said it would “carry greater symbolic significance”, because the excess supply of dollars from exporters is larger than the ratio can absorb [1]. It also reverses the bank’s September 2023 cut, made when the problem was a falling yuan [1]. For you, the dull lesson is that a currency is a queue of invoices. When exporters bring home more dollars than anyone wants, the price moves, and a central bank can slow it but rarely stop it. Nothing here is investment advice.

up-to-25-billion-in-bonds-a-third-in-eur.title: Up to $25 billion in bonds, a third in euros, days after a negative outlook
up-to-25-billion-in-bonds-a-third-in-eur.dek: Meta goes to the debt market for the AI build, and for the first time asks European investors too.
up-to-25-billion-in-bonds-a-third-in-eur.text: Meta set out on Tuesday to raise $20 billion to $25 billion in bonds, two-thirds in dollars and one-third in euros, according to people familiar with the deal cited by CNBC [1]. It comes days after S&P Global Ratings moved Meta’s outlook to AA- negative from AA- stable, citing “uncertainty” about heavy capital spending and negative free cash flow [1]. The invoices are large. Meta expects $135 billion to $145 billion of capital spending this year, posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion last quarter, raised $25 billion in bonds in April, and last week announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity [1]. Desk arithmetic: at the top of the range, this sale plus April’s would be $50 billion of bonds in a year. A rating outlook is the dull line that tells you what lenders will charge for it. Nothing here is investment advice.

ordinary-ledger-a-fuel-price-cap-with-th.title: Ordinary Ledger: a fuel price cap with three tripwires, no formula and no promised cent
ordinary-ledger-a-fuel-price-cap-with-th.dek: The economy ministry's first draft of the 'Kraftstoffhöchstpreisgesetz' is out. It tells you when a cap could apply, and almost nothing about how high it would be.
ordinary-ledger-a-fuel-price-cap-with-th.text: If you drive, two dates on your calendar now belong together. The tank rebate of roughly 17 cents a litre ends on 31 December, and the coalition agreed in September that a fuel price cap should follow on 1 January 2027 [2]. On Monday evening tagesschau reported that the economy ministry’s first draft of that law had reached the ARD’s Berlin studio [1]. It is a careful document, and it is careful mostly about when the cap should not apply. The ledger. - Trigger: petrol and diesel must each rise by more than five percentage points above the average price increase in the other EU states, for three weeks in a row, on European Commission figures [1][2]. - Who checks: the fuel market transparency unit at the Bundeskartellamt, every week [2]. - What it is called: a crisis instrument “in the most extreme emergency”, set by government ordinance [1]. - How long: three months at most, and it can be suspended if supply is at risk [1]. - Where: the federal states may set their own, higher or lower, ceilings, even for individual districts, according to the ADAC’s reading of the draft [1][2]. - How high: not stated. The formula is left to a later ordinance, and the ministry says the law can promise “neither the level of a possible maximum price nor a guaranteed price cut” [2]. Why it is built like this. The ministry’s worry, as it told dpa, is that a cap set too low could make deliveries unprofitable, so that “imports could fail to arrive” [1]. The model is Belgium and Luxembourg, where a formula has capped pump prices since a 1974 agreement in Belgium’s case; there the ceiling moves with crude and transport costs and stops excessive mark-ups, not high prices [2]. The ADAC expects a cap to trim daily average prices “at most slightly” and warns against inflated hopes [2]. The politics, in one line each. Saarland’s premier Anke Rehlinger (SPD) called the draft “a fuel-price-cap prevention law”, because three weeks is a long time to wait [1]. The SPD’s economic spokesman in the Bundestag, Sebastian Roloff, says it is not what the coalition agreed [1]. The draft is only in early coordination inside the government [1]. At your tank. Nothing changes this week. Budget for January as if the rebate simply ends, because that is the one date already fixed [2]; treat any cap as a possible brake on spikes, not a discount. Until 31 December the cheapest move remains the dull one: under the rule that lets stations raise prices only once a day at 12:00, the ADAC advises filling up shortly before noon [3]. Nothing here is investment advice.

2-9-again-the-health-insurance-add-on-ho.title: 2.9% again: the health insurance add-on holds for 2027, and the minister calls it a first step
2-9-again-the-health-insurance-add-on-ho.dek: The health ministry has fixed next year's average supplementary contribution at this year's level. Your own fund still sets your rate.
2-9-again-the-health-insurance-add-on-ho.text: One line on next year’s payslip has stopped climbing, at least on paper. The Federal Health Ministry has set the average supplementary contribution rate in statutory health insurance for 2027 at 2.9%, unchanged from this year [1]. The figure rests on the October estimate of the official forecasting group, the GKV-Schätzerkreis, which met on 14 October [1]. Average is not yours. Each health fund decides its own supplementary rate [1]. The 2.9% is a benchmark, so the number that matters is the one in your fund’s letter. Desk arithmetic: on a gross monthly salary of €3,500, 2.9% comes to €101.50, which employer and employee normally share. Why it held. The ministry credits a law to stabilise contributions, which it says will relieve the funds by up to €19 billion next year [1]. Spending is expected to rise by less than 3% in 2027, after almost 7% this year; for the first time in three years, the ministry says, rising income would cover rising spending [1]. The minister’s own caveat. “That can only be a first step,” said Health Minister Carsten Linnemann; a finance commission is due to propose structural reforms by the end of 2026 [1]. That is the right order: a held rate first, then the harder question of what the system costs. You do not need to do anything today. When your fund writes to you about 2027, compare its rate with 2.9%. Nothing here is financial advice.

ihre-mailservice-verwaltungscenter-the-p.title: 'Ihre Mailservice VerwaltungsCenter': the pension fund did not send that
ihre-mailservice-verwaltungscenter-the-p.dek: Consumer advisers warn of a fake e-mail in the name of the Deutsche Rentenversicherung that asks you to 'check' your details.
ihre-mailservice-verwaltungscenter-the-p.text: The Verbraucherzentrale is warning about an e-mail with the subject line “Ihre Mailservice VerwaltungsCenter” that pretends to come from the Deutsche Rentenversicherung [1]. It asks you to review and complete your details in the pension portal, citing supposedly new EU rules on storing personal data, and offers a link to do it [1]. The tells are the usual ones: no personal greeting, an odd sender address, and a link [1]. Do not click it, do not reply, and move the message to spam [1]. If you want to check your pension account, go to the Rentenversicherung’s official website yourself [1]. A real institution does not need you to hurry.

search-off-by-default-and-no-search-with.title: Search off by default, and no Search without the AI in it
search-off-by-default-and-no-search-with.dek: Google handed schools a switch for its AI. The switch has three positions, and the last one turns off Search as well.
search-off-by-default-and-no-search-with.text: On Tuesday morning Google announced that its AI products would be switched off by default for students in schools that use its education software. Until then, its Gemini tools had been on automatically for schools using Google Classroom [1]. Chris Phillips, who runs Google’s education business, wrote that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search “will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on” [1]. The catch was in the last item. Search was on the list. After what NBC News called “significant backlash”, Google clarified later on Tuesday that schools can switch on Search alone, without the other Gemini products [1]. But Search itself now carries AI features, such as AI-generated summaries, so a school cannot have Google Search without them [1]. Google said the changes “give schools more choice, not less”, and that AI Mode and AI Overviews will walk students through problems step by step rather than hand over answers [1]. Critics were not persuaded. Randi Weingarten of the American Federation of Teachers said Google had “prioritized its business interests over the education of our children” [1]. Josh Golin of the advocacy group Fairplay said Google was trying “to strong-arm schools into using its AI products” [1]. Dozens of outlets covered the announcement within hours, Techmeme’s roundup shows [2]. Two dull facts matter more than the quotes. First, Google’s reach: most Chromebooks are bought by school districts, and nearly two-thirds of assignments used a Google product, according to a 2023 Schoolytics report cited by NBC [1]. Second, the evidence: Stanford’s SCALE Initiative says there are no high-quality causal studies into student use of AI [1]. A product used that widely, with that thin a research base, is exactly the kind of decision schools should make slowly, by procurement rule and parent meeting rather than by default setting. The constructive part is that schools now have a switch, and someone in each district must decide where to put it. That is the institution doing its job. For you, if you have a child at school, the useful question for the next parents’ evening is simple: which of the three positions did our school choose, and why?

27-of-america-s-data-centre-gigawatts-an.title: 27% of America's data-centre gigawatts, and a governor's race that decides the permits
27-of-america-s-data-centre-gigawatts-an.dek: Wall Street spent election day studying Texas, where the AI build-out meets water bills and a moratorium.
27-of-america-s-data-centre-gigawatts-an.text: The AI boom is usually described in chips. On election day, analysts described it in Texas permits. Wells Fargo estimates that 27% of US data-centre gigawatts are in Texas alone, CNBC reports [1]. More than 80% of Texas voters say they worry about data centres’ effect on water supply and electricity prices, according to a University of Houston survey of 2,000 likely voters conducted 10–14 October [1]. The state already has a pause. Governor Greg Abbott halted data-centre permitting in September, saying “Texans must come first” [1]. He sought a fourth term against the Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Evercore ISI, citing its colleague Sarah Bianchi, wrote that Abbott is likely to lift the moratorium, while Hinojosa is expected to keep it [1]. In the Senate race, the Democrat James Talarico has proposed ending some tax subsidies and tightening standards on labour, the environment and grid use, according to The Texas Tribune as cited by CNBC [1]. Not every analyst reads a Democratic advance as bad for the industry. Rob Rains of Washington Analysis expects a Democratic Congress to push harder to “fence off” Chinese competitors [1]. TD Cowen’s Paul Gallant expects President Trump to veto any AI safety law that creates “material risk to the AI trade” [1]. The useful point survives whatever the count shows by the time you read this. Data centres are no longer only a technology story. They are a water story, a grid story and a ballot story, decided by permits, tariffs and voters, which is how big infrastructure has always been built.

19-9-billion-of-sales-and-434-million-of.title: $19.9 billion of sales, and $434 million of cash out of the door
19-9-billion-of-sales-and-434-million-of.dek: Super Micro's record quarter shows how an AI server boom looks in the dullest statement: the cash flow.
19-9-billion-of-sales-and-434-million-of.text: Super Micro, which builds AI servers, reported record quarterly sales of $19.9 billion, against $5.0 billion a year earlier, and net income of $1.59 billion [1]. It expects $72 billion to $82 billion of sales in the fiscal year to June [1]. The cash-flow statement tells the other half. Operations used $434 million of cash in the quarter [1]. Money owed by customers rose to $9.69 billion from $6.13 billion in June, and inventories to $15.05 billion from $12.90 billion [1]. Desk arithmetic: those two lines grew by about $5.7 billion in three months, partly offset by $3.05 billion more in customer prepayments [1]. The figures are preliminary and unaudited, the company says [1]. Profit is an opinion until the invoices are paid. Nothing here is investment advice.

300-before-anyone-audits-the-surgery-and.title: €300 before anyone audits the surgery, and seven in ten checks would go
300-before-anyone-audits-the-surgery-and.dek: A draft law seen by the Deutsches Ärzteblatt would spare doctors, hospitals and insurers some €100 million of paperwork a year. Most of it is the dull kind, which is the point.
300-before-anyone-audits-the-surgery-and.text: A health service runs on two things: people who treat you, and paper that proves they did. A draft law from the Federal Health Ministry, seen by the Deutsches Ärzteblatt, goes after the second. It carries the unlovely name Hilfsmittelmodernisierungs- und Bürokratierückbaugesetz, and the ministry puts the saving at about €100 million a year, rising to about €180 million a year from 2030 [1]. The headline change is small and concrete. Insurers would no longer be able to request an efficiency audit of a practice for sums below €300, counted per practice site, per quarter and per insurer [1]. Doctors’ bodies, among them the KBV and the German Medical Association, have asked for such a threshold for years. The ministry expects about 70% of the audit procedures carried out so far to fall away [1]. Desk arithmetic: seven in ten fewer procedures means seven in ten fewer letters, replies and files on both sides of the desk. Psychotherapy for the young gets its own line. Therapists who mainly or only treat children and adolescents would form a separate group in the planning of where practices may open, so places can be steered to where the need is [1]. Applying for short-term therapy would go from two steps to one, and a digital application and review procedure would be added [1]. Hospitals would drop several reports: the detailed staffing data for psychiatric and psychosomatic units, the proof of how extra money for nurses’ pay rises was spent, and the InEK extreme-cost report [1]. Quality-assurance data would follow a once-only rule, so a provider reports a figure once rather than once per procedure [1]. Insurers would file reports on bonus programmes every five years instead of every three [1]. None of this is law yet, and drafts change on their way through. But the direction is the right one. A threshold, a single form and a report nobody reads anymore struck off: that is how a system gets its staff back, one quarter at a time.

one-injection-one-visit-who-writes-the.title: One injection, one visit: WHO writes the specification for TB medicines nobody has yet
one-injection-one-visit-who-writes-the.dek: Most tuberculosis treatment still means months of daily pills. WHO has now told developers what a long-acting injection would have to do to replace them.
one-injection-one-visit-who-writes-the.text: Tuberculosis is usually cured with tablets. The trouble is the calendar: most prevention and treatment programmes rely on daily oral medicines taken over several months, and keeping that up is hard for patients and for the clinics that follow them [1]. On Tuesday the World Health Organization published target regimen profiles for long-acting injectable medicines, a list of what such products would have to achieve [1]. For prevention, the target is a complete course in a single injection, given at one visit to a health worker [1]. For active disease, WHO wants a regimen of no more than four months with three dosing visits or fewer [1]. Both profiles ask for small injection volumes, products that need no cold chain, injections that trained staff can give at the lowest feasible level of the health system, and safety and efficacy comparable to today’s pills [1]. “Long-acting injectables could make TB prevention and treatment much simpler for the people who need them,” said Tereza Kasaeva, who leads WHO’s HIV, TB, hepatitis and STI department [1]. The profiles were drawn up with regulators, national TB programmes, people who have had TB and civil society groups, after a public consultation in April and May [1]. Several candidates are entering or approaching clinical development [1]. WHO also says work on better oral regimens should continue, so that patients keep a choice [1]. A specification is not a medicine. It is the drawing that comes before the factory, and the people who will pay for the factory now know what to build.

a-tongue-swab-for-people-who-cannot-coug.title: A tongue swab for people who cannot cough up a sample
a-tongue-swab-for-people-who-cannot-coug.dek: WHO's new tuberculosis diagnosis guidelines add tests that work closer to the patient, and a way to test several samples at once.
a-tongue-swab-for-people-who-cannot-coug.text: Testing for tuberculosis has long depended on sputum, the phlegm coughed up from the lungs. Many people, children among them, cannot produce it. The second edition of WHO’s guidelines on TB diagnosis, published on 3 November, recommends tongue swabs as a new sample type for exactly those people [1]. The 167-page document also recommends a new class of near point-of-care tests that let clinics at the edges of a health system diagnose TB, and pooling of sputum samples to test for TB and rifampicin resistance more cheaply where resources are exceptionally tight [1]. A living website will list the recommended tests and their prequalification status, and operational guidance is due in the coming months [1]. The cheapest test is the one that reaches the patient.

nine-ships-in-24-days-317-in-six-months-.title: Nine ships in 24 days, 317 in six months, and a $40 billion counter-drone bill
nine-ships-in-24-days-317-in-six-months-.dek: The Black Sea war is reaching NATO's coastline. Romania and Bulgaria are answering with forensic patience and patrol aircraft, not slogans.
nine-ships-in-24-days-317-in-six-months-.text: Between 5 and 28 October, nine merchant vessels were struck or caught up in drone-linked incidents off Bulgaria and Romania, five near Bulgaria and four near Romania, according to a timeline compiled by the Bulgarian agency BGNES [2]. Several sank, and crew died or are missing [2]. NATO said in October that it would send maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to the area [1]. The strikes continued anyway. On 28 October the Liberian-flagged container ship Contship Jet, sailing from Haifa to Constanța with 421 containers, was hit by three maritime drones about 17 nautical miles east of Cape Kaliakra and sank. All 18 crew were rescued and taken to Varna [2]. The wider numbers are worse. Russia and Ukraine hit 317 merchant and other vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov between May and October, against 74 in the previous half-year, according to Ambrey Analytics [1]. In October, Ambrey counted 38 Russian strikes on ships and 5 Ukrainian ones [1]. Desk arithmetic: 317 is about 4.3 times 74. Trade is paying for it. Ukraine’s grain exports through its ports fell to 0.81 million tonnes in September, from 2.1 million a year earlier [1]. Military analysts told Reuters they had little doubt the attacks near Romania and Bulgaria were Russian. Moscow denies targeting Ukraine’s neighbours [1]. What stands out is how carefully the two NATO governments handle attribution. Bucharest calls the strikes on civilian ships “systematic” but has not attributed individual attacks, citing the need for forensic evidence. Sofia says some attacks appear to benefit Russia but has not blamed it [1]. That can look timid. In fact it is what makes a later case hold up. Romania’s defence ministry has documented at least six incursion episodes involving nine aerial targets between 14 and 31 October [2]. The response is mostly about procurement, not rhetoric. A NATO official said the alliance had already committed to invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years [1]. A senior Romanian official pointed to an urgent need for surface-to-air interceptors and radars [1]. Turkey, which controls the straits, is waiting for Moscow and Kyiv to respond to its proposal for a narrow maritime ceasefire [1]. If you ship through Constanța, or insure cargo that does, the useful information is in the incident log: coordinates, distance from shore, cargo manifests. Leave the communiqués aside. Read the log.

tech-on-the-cheap-britain-s-cyber-chief-.title: "Tech on the cheap": Britain's cyber chief sends the bill for old servers
tech-on-the-cheap-britain-s-cyber-chief-.dek: The NCSC's annual review says AI did not create the weaknesses. It is finding the ones we left lying around.
tech-on-the-cheap-britain-s-cyber-chief-.text: Launching the National Cyber Security Centre’s annual review on Tuesday, its chief executive, Richard Horne, warned of the “real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents” in the coming months [1]. He pinned the risk on the backlog, not on clever new attacks: “vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable” [1]. The evidence is in the patch notes. Major technology providers are now fixing hundreds of vulnerabilities in a single update, and the Linux kernel project alone patched more than a thousand last month, Horne said [1]. The NCSC judges it “highly likely” that AI-powered malware will be used in a ransomware attack on Britain’s critical infrastructure by 2028 [1]. Even state-linked hacks, it says, often succeed through internet-facing applications where patches were available but were not deployed in time [1]. Horne’s sharpest line was aimed at the boardroom. “For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap,” he said, pointing to end-of-life systems kept running for “cost efficiency” [1]. The defence is mostly budget lines. A £70 million NERV Centre will use AI to look for vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure. A further £60 million goes to the first phase of Cyber Shield, a national network of AI defence agents [1]. The NCSC still believes the “structural advantage will remain with defenders”, because they own the environment, but it says that advantage “is not a given” [1]. The one thing to do this week is unglamorous: list what you run that no longer gets updates, and give it a retirement date.

eight-phones-some-ammunition-and-a-third.title: Eight phones, some ammunition, and a third arrest over a Starlink fire
eight-phones-some-ammunition-and-a-third.dek: Hybrid sabotage is being met the slow way, with warrants and extradition files.
eight-phones-some-ammunition-and-a-third.text: Special police units have arrested a Turkish national in the Reutlingen district. Baden-Württemberg’s criminal police office says he instructed two men to set fire to a Starlink ground station in Poland on the night of 23 September [1]. He is held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist offence, and eight mobile phones and ammunition were seized [1]. The two alleged arsonists, arrested in Nürtingen in mid-October, face extradition to Poland [1]. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk has called the fire an “act of hybrid warfare” [2]. Warsaw suspects Russian intelligence was behind it [1]. Starlink is a strategically important part of Ukraine’s defence [1]. A warrant is a quieter answer than a speech, and a more durable one.

two-cyclones-in-a-week-on-the-same-coast.title: Two cyclones in a week on the same coast, and 12,230 people in shelters rather than in the water
two-cyclones-in-a-week-on-the-same-coast.dek: Murasu hit Andhra Pradesh days after Arnab. It killed two people and flattened crops on 52,459 hectares; the evacuations, the train cancellations and the shelters did the quiet work.
two-cyclones-in-a-week-on-the-same-coast.text: The Bay of Bengal has sent Andhra Pradesh two cyclones in a week. Severe cyclonic storm Murasu came ashore near Ongole in Prakasam district in the early hours of Tuesday, local time, days after Cyclone Arnab hit the same region and neighbouring Odisha [1][2]. The India Meteorological Department put the maximum sustained wind at landfall at 110–120 km/h [1]. The ledger of damage is specific, and so far small in lives. At least two people died in Bapatla district when buildings collapsed on them, the state disaster management authority’s managing director, Prakhar Jain, told The Hindu [1]. Standing crops on 52,459 hectares were destroyed, 312 houses were damaged, and more than 200 mobile towers were affected [1]. Preliminary reports put losses at ₹344 crore, which Jain said was less severe than Arnab’s toll [1]. More than 35 trains were cancelled, 14 diverted and eight rescheduled [1]. The rain fell on parched ground, and then on too much of it. Prakasam and Bapatla received around 200 millimetres between midnight and 06:00 local time [1]. Later in the day Marripalem in Palnadu district recorded 263.75 millimetres and Ganapavaram 246.7; five stations measured “extremely heavy” rainfall above 204.5 millimetres and 21 more topped 100 [1]. In neighbouring Telangana, where the IMD had issued a red alert, Bhadradri Kothagudem recorded 6.5 centimetres [3]. The machinery that does not make headlines. Officials began evacuating on Monday, planning to move about 30,000 people, and 12,230 were still in relief centres on Tuesday evening [1][2]. In Kothapatnam about 400 fishing families were moved out before the storm hit, one fisherman told PTI [2]. Hyderabad’s traffic police asked employers to send staff home early or let them work from home [3]. A storm that hits a coast twice in a week tests whether the second response is faster than the first. On Tuesday’s evidence, the shelters were ready. Murasu weakened into a cyclonic storm by midday and was forecast to become a deep depression overnight as it moved north-west towards Telangana [1]. If you have family or business in the region, the useful sources this week are the IMD’s district warnings and the state disaster authority, not the rumours that travel faster than either.

fifth-sunniest-october-13-more-rain-and-.title: Fifth-sunniest October, 13% more rain, and a drought that is still there
fifth-sunniest-october-13-more-rain-and-.dek: Britain's provisional October figures are a lesson in why one wet month does not refill a hot summer. Now high pressure has switched the rain off again.
fifth-sunniest-october-13-more-rain-and-.text: October in Britain managed to be wetter, warmer and sunnier than average at the same time. Provisional Met Office figures show the UK received 13% more rain than in a typical October, with northern Scotland 31% above its long-term average [1]. It was also the fifth-sunniest October since records began in 1910, and the mean temperature was 0.9°C above average, the ninth month in a row above the norm [1]. The rain came in a rush. Most of it fell in the last third of the month, when Storms Austen and Boelo swept through; 24 October was provisionally the UK’s joint-sixth wettest day on record [1]. England had its wettest week in two years, the Environment Agency said, but warned that it was not enough to ease the drought left by the hottest summer on record [1]. Sustained above-average rain will be needed through the winter [1]. Then the tap closed. High pressure has taken control and the jet stream has moved north, so the first days of November are largely dry, with frost and fog at night in the north and west and a brisk easterly in the south [1]. The BBC’s forecasters see a weak low drifting up from France at the weekend and, beyond next week, a likely return of Atlantic systems, with “a lot of uncertainty” and no definite storm in sight [1]. The lesson is the reservoir manager’s, not the headline writer’s: a drought is a balance sheet, and one good month is a deposit, not a repayment.

embargoed-until-9-november-the-year-s-cl.title: Embargoed until 9 November: the year's climate report card
embargoed-until-9-november-the-year-s-cl.dek: The WMO has set a date for its State of the Climate 2026 update, as Antalya readies for COP31. One of its inputs, a very strong El Niño forecast, is already public.
embargoed-until-9-november-the-year-s-cl.text: The report has a date; you just cannot read it yet. The World Meteorological Organization will brief journalists in Geneva on Friday 6 November on its State of the Climate 2026 update, under embargo until 9 November [1]. Secretary-General Celeste Saulo and the WMO’s head of climate information, John Kennedy, are listed to present it [1]. In Antalya, COP31 organisers expect around 50,000 visitors a day in the Blue Zone and have brought in 630 low-emission buses [3]. One input is already public. The WMO’s October seasonal update expects the Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly to reach about +3.8°C over November to January, peaking around December, with a narrow spread between models [2]. An embargo is not secrecy. It is a timetable, and timetables are how institutions keep their promises.

de-power-day-ahead-04nov.title: Wednesday ends the €250 streak, by €1.01
de-power-day-ahead-04nov.subtitle: Germany/Luxembourg day-ahead electricity price, daily average by delivery day, € per MWh
de-power-day-ahead-04nov.source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, day-ahead price DE-LU (filter 4169), delivery days 1 Sep to 4 Nov 2026, retrieved 4 Nov 2026 · CC BY 4.0
de-power-day-ahead-04nov.alt: Line chart of the daily average German-Luxembourg day-ahead electricity price from 1 September to 4 November 2026, in euros per megawatt hour. It falls to €30.12 on Saturday 24 October and €13.12 on Sunday 25 October during the storm, then climbs to €314.85 on Thursday 29 October, the highest daily average of 2026 so far. The six delivery days from 29 October to 3 November all stayed above €250, ending with €252.85 on Tuesday 3 November. The latest value is €248.99 for delivery on Wednesday 4 November.

ust-election-day-04nov.title: Election day closed at 4.61% and 4.95%
ust-election-day-04nov.subtitle: US 2-year and 10-year Treasury par yields, daily close, 1 Oct to 3 Nov 2026, %
ust-election-day-04nov.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates, 2-year and 10-year, 1 Oct to 3 Nov 2026 (home.treasury.gov), retrieved 4 Nov 2026 · U.S. government data, public domain · Official closes only; overnight moves after the election are not drawn.
ust-election-day-04nov.alt: Line chart of the daily US 2-year and 10-year Treasury par yields from 1 October to 3 November 2026. On 1 October the 2-year is at 4.78% and the 10-year at 5.24%. The 10-year peaks at 5.31% on 5 October; both fall sharply on 22 October and drift lower to 4.56% and 4.94% on 30 October. On Tuesday 3 November 2026, US election day and the latest value, the 2-year closes at 4.61% and the 10-year at 4.95%, a gap of 0.34 percentage points.

us-senate-seats-04nov.alt: Bar chart of the 100 US Senate seats by status at 05:14 CET on Wednesday 4 November 2026, per NBC News projections on AP data: 34 Democratic seats not up this year and 15 Democratic projected winners on Tuesday (49 in total, including four flips), 31 Republican seats not up and 8 Republican projected winners (39 in total), and 12 races not yet projected. A majority is 51.
